Validated Key Findings
Overall Diabetes Prevalence
8.82%
8,482 of 96,146 patients in the analytical cohort are diabetic — a class imbalance typical of epidemiological data.
HbA1c Cohort Gap
+1.57 pp
Diabetic patients average 6.96% HbA1c vs 5.39% for controls — the strongest observed clinical association (r ≈ 0.41).
Blood Glucose Gap
+61.21 mg/dL
Diabetic patients average 194.03 mg/dL vs 132.82 mg/dL for controls (r ≈ 0.42).
BMI Gap
~+4.6 kg/m²
Diabetic patients show higher average BMI (≈31.5) vs controls (≈26.9).
Age Gap
~+21 years
Diabetic patients average ≈60.9 years vs ≈39.9 years for controls.
Comorbidity Escalation
6.1× increase
Prevalence rises from 6.40% (no comorbidities) to 39.13% (both hypertension & heart disease).
High-Risk Segment
33.74%
Age 66+ × Obese patients show 3.8× the overall prevalence — a priority segment for further investigation.
Data Quality
0 missing
No missing values; 3,854 duplicates removed (3.85%) to form the 96,146-record analytical cohort.
Strongest Correlates
HbA1c, Glucose
Pearson correlations with diabetes: HbA1c ≈ 0.41, blood glucose ≈ 0.42 — the top observed clinical associations.
Recommendations
  • 1
    Monitor elevated-prevalence segments. Prioritize patients in the Age 66+ × Obese segment and those with both hypertension and heart disease, where observed diabetes prevalence exceeds 33–39%.
  • 2
    Focus on HbA1c and blood glucose. These are the strongest observed clinical associations with diabetes. Treat them as primary screening indicators in any downstream predictive modeling effort.
  • 3
    Examine comorbidity combinations. The 6.1× escalation from no comorbidities to both conditions suggests compounding risk. Investigate care pathways for patients with dual cardiovascular conditions.
  • 4
    Improve smoking-history completeness. 34.2% of records carry "No Info". Improving data capture for smoking history would strengthen lifestyle-based segmentation in future analyses.
  • 5
    Consider predictive modeling. The validated EDA provides a strong foundation. A supervised model (e.g., gradient boosting) using HbA1c, glucose, BMI, age, and comorbidity flags is a logical next analytical phase.
  • 6
    Preserve "No Info" as a category. Do not impute "No Info" smoking records as "never" — the report treats this as a distinct information status.

Methodology & Assumptions

  1. Duplicate records were removed according to the validated analysis (3,854 rows purged).
  2. The final analytical cohort contains 96,146 records after deduplication.
  3. No missing values were identified in the source data.
  4. Engineered categories (Age Group, BMI Category, Blood Glucose Category, Comorbidity Group) are derived analytical groupings — not original dataset fields.
  5. Extreme-value treatment follows the validated analysis where applicable: winsorization at the 1st and 99th percentiles retains density while bounding variance.
  6. All results represent observed associations, not causal conclusions. No medical diagnoses are made.
  7. The dataset contains no time field — no genuine temporal trend is fabricated. Distributions represent population segmentation.
  8. "No Info" in smoking history is preserved as a distinct information category.
  9. No unsupported metrics (product, sales, revenue, customer) are introduced. This is a health/clinical dataset.
  10. Benchmark values (8.82%, 6.96%, 194.03, etc.) originate from the validated EDA report and are used as reconciliation references — the dashboard computes all values directly from the source data.
